1.note: The word translated as **to** appears in the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense, especially when compared with other verses in this chapter that introduce the descendants of other sons of Jacob (verses 13, 14, 20, and 30). Scholars have proposed that, influenced by the frequent occurrence of the phrase “to the sons of” in the previous chapter, a scribe may inadvertently added the word “to” here. If there is a major Bible translation in your area and it does not represent the word “to,” you may wish to do the same in your translation. Alternate translation: [And the sons of Issachar]

2.q: גִּבּ֥וֹרֵי חַ֖יִל לְ⁠תֹלְדוֹתָ֑⁠ם מִסְפָּרָ⁠ם֙ בִּ⁠ימֵ֣י דָוִ֔יד עֶשְׂרִֽים־וּ⁠שְׁנַ֥יִם אֶ֖לֶף וְ⁠שֵׁ֥שׁ מֵאֽוֹת
2.note: The expression **by their generations** seems to be a short form of the phrase “in their being enrolled by their generations” that occurs in 5:7. To translate the expression here and the similar ones in verses 4 and 9, see how you translated the phrase there. Alternate translation: [Their genealogies record 22,600 of them as warriors of valor in the days of David]
The author is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [during the reign of David]

4.q: וַ⁠עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֨ם לְ⁠תֹלְדוֹתָ֜⁠ם לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אֲבוֹתָ֗⁠ם גְּדוּדֵי֙ צְבָ֣א מִלְחָמָ֔ה שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וְ⁠שִׁשָּׁ֖ה אָ֑לֶף כִּֽי־הִרְבּ֥וּ נָשִׁ֖ים וּ⁠בָנִֽים
4.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since they multiplied wives and sons, with them, according to their generations in the house of their fathers, were warriors of an army of battle, 36,000]
The pronoun **they** refers to the five men mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Izrahaiah and his sons multiplied]

5.note: The author is using the plural **valors** where he could have used the singular form. This suggests that he is using the plural form to emphasize the great courage and skill of these **warriors**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express the emphasis in another way, here and in verses 7, 11, and 40. Alternate translation: [very great warriors]

The expression **enrolled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language, here and in verses 7, 9, and 40. The UST models one way to do that.

6.note: In the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today, this verse begins with the word **Benjamin**. However, a comparison with the other verses in the chapter that introduce the descendants of one of Jacob’s sons suggest that it should begin “The sons of Benjamin.” Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have inadvertently omitted the expression “The sons of” because it consists of the same two consonants as the beginning of the name Benjamin, which may have been written as a separate word. (In other words, rather than writing BN BN YMN, a scribe may simply have written BN YMN.) If there is a major Bible translation in your area and expands the start of this verse accordingly, you may wish to do the same in your translation. Alternate translation: [The sons of Benjamin]

12.note: The term that the ULT translates as **Aher** could be: (1) the name of a man. The ULT and UST follow that interpretation. (2) a term that means “another.” That other son of Jacob would be Dan, since Genesis 46:23 indicates that Dan had a son named Hushim. The reference in the next verse to the “sons of Bilhah” would support this interpretation, since the two sons of Bilhah were Dan and Naphtali. The author would be reluctant to name Dan because that was the earliest Israelite tribe to become involved in idolatry. Alternate translation: [another son of Jacob] or [Dan]

13.note: While the first instance of the term **sons** is literal, in the second instance, the author is using the term to mean “descendants.” Bilhah was the mother of Naphtali, so the other four men are her grandsons. Alternate translation: [descendants of Bilhah] or [grandsons of Bilhah]

15.note: The author is using the adjective **second** as a noun to mean a particular person, the second son of **Machir**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [his second son]

16.note: See how you translated this expression in 4:9. Alternate translation: [and she named him Peresh]

20.note: The term **sons** means “descendants” here, but the term “son” throughout this verse and the next verse is literal. Alternate translation: [And the descendants of Ephraim]

21.q: וַ⁠הֲרָג֗וּ⁠ם אַנְשֵׁי־גַת֙ הַ⁠נּוֹלָדִ֣ים בָּ⁠אָ֔רֶץ כִּ֣י יָרְד֔וּ לָ⁠קַ֖חַת אֶת־מִקְנֵי⁠הֶֽם
21.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [But because they came down to take their livestock, the men of Gath born in the land killed them]

The expression ** born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. The UST models one way to do that.

23.note: The author is referring in a polite way to a private activity, sexual relations, by using the phrase **went in to**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [And he slept with his wife]

23.q: וַ⁠יִּקְרָ֤א אֶת־שְׁמ⁠וֹ֙ בְּרִיעָ֔ה כִּ֥י בְ⁠רָעָ֖ה הָיְתָ֥ה בְּ⁠בֵיתֽ⁠וֹ
23.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because disaster was in his house, he called his name Beriah]
See how you translated this expression in 4:9. Alternate translation: [And he named him Beriah]

25.note: The pronoun **his** refers in this instance to Ephraim. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Rephah was Ephraim’s son]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. (It is also possible that a scribe inadvertently omitted these words.) You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and Resheph, his son]

27.note: The man whom the author calls **Non** here is called “Nun” in all other contexts in the Bible. Recall whether your translation team decided to use the same name for a given person in each instance where it appears or whether you decided to use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [Nun]

28.note: To translate the term **daughters** here and in the rest of this verse and in the next verse, see how you translated the term in 2:23. Alternate translation: [were Bethel and its surrounding villages]

29.note: Since people’s hands are at their sides, the author is using the term **hands** to mean the sides or borders of the territory that belonged to the descendants of Manasseh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And along the borders of the tribe of Manasseh]

While Ephriam (v. 20) and Manasseh (v. 14) were both **sons of Joseph**, the author is describing the “holdings” and “dwellings” (v. 28) of the descendants of Ephraim, so here he means the descendants of Joseph through Ephraim. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Joseph, the son of Israel, through Ephraim]

37.note: Many interpreters believe that **Ithran** may be another name for “Jether,” since he is mentioned at the start of the next verse. However, we do not recommend that you use the name “Jether” in the text of your translation, since it does not appear here in any Hebrew manuscript or ancient version. You may wish to indicate this possibility in a footnote.

40.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:17. Alternate translation: [Officials enrolled them]
